modules.title: Conservative Newtonian systems and determinism
modules.doc:
Conservative Newtonian systems: a locally Lipschitz force gives determinism.

## i. Overview

A conservative Newtonian system is a point mass `m` in a configuration space `X` under a
potential `V`, with equation of motion `m r̈ = -∇V(r)`. Physics takes for granted that position
and velocity at one instant fix the motion at all instants. This file makes that a theorem and
states what it costs.

The main result is `NewtonianSystem.isDeterministic_of_hasLocallyLipschitzForce`: if the force
is locally Lipschitz, two solutions with the same position and velocity at one instant coincide
at every instant; in the form usually quoted,
`NewtonianSystem.isDeterministic_of_hasC2Potential`, a `C²` potential suffices. Continuity of
the force is not enough: the Norton dome has a continuous force and a `C¹` potential, and a
particle at rest on its apex may stay or leave at any time (see `NortonDome.Determinism`).

The `NewtonianSystem` defined here asks only for a differentiable potential, the least under
which the equation of motion makes sense. Newton's laws, as stated, are silent on how regular
the force must be, and the dome shows that without some regularity the equation does not
determine the motion. A definition that is to be deterministic must add something the laws do
not state, a regularity condition on the force or a restriction on the admissible motions;
whether that is part of the theory or a choice about it is debated. Each candidate condition is
a separate predicate, so that what it buys is a theorem, and the file takes no side. The
predicates are:

- `IsDeterministic`: position and velocity at one instant fix the solution.
- `SatisfiesFirstLaw`: a body at rest where the force vanishes stays at rest. It follows from
  determinism and is the form of the first law the dome violates. The interval reading follows
  from the second law for every system (`IsSolution.deriv_eq_of_force_eq_zero_on`, section B.3).
- `HasLocallyLipschitzForce`: the hypothesis of the ODE uniqueness theorem. `HasLipschitzForce`
  and `HasC2Potential` are the stronger conditions usually assumed; each implies it and neither
  implies the other.
- `HasLocalSolutions`: existence, kept separate. For a continuous force on a finite-dimensional
  configuration space it follows from Peano's theorem, whose proof is pending in Mathlib;
  section E derives it from the statement in `NortonDome.PeanoExistence`, informally.

The proof of determinism turns the equation of motion into the first-order system
`(r, v)' = (v, F(r)/m)` on `X × X`, applies Mathlib's local uniqueness theorem for integral
curves, and extends to all time by connectedness of the real line. So continuity buys
existence and local Lipschitz continuity buys uniqueness; the file records what each condition
does, not which one is right.

## ii. Key results

- `NewtonianSystem.isDeterministic_of_hasLocallyLipschitzForce`: a locally Lipschitz force
  gives determinism, hence `NewtonianSystem.satisfiesFirstLaw_of_hasLocallyLipschitzForce`
  the first law. `NewtonianSystem.isDeterministic_of_hasC2Potential` and
  `NewtonianSystem.isDeterministic_of_hasLipschitzForce` are the forms usually quoted; the
  chain of implications is drawn in section D.3.
- `NewtonianSystem.ODE_solution_unique_of_locallyLipschitz`: integral curves of a locally
  Lipschitz vector field through a common point coincide for all time.
- `NewtonianSystem`, `NewtonianSystem.force`, `NewtonianSystem.EquationOfMotion` and
  `NewtonianSystem.IsSolution`: the system, the force `-∇V`, Newton's second law, and its
  twice differentiable solutions; `NewtonianSystem.isSolution_const` is rest at an
  equilibrium.
- `NewtonianSystem.IsSolution.deriv_eq_of_force_eq_zero_on`: the first law read on an
  interval, a consequence of the second law for every system.
- `NewtonianSystem.IsDeterministic`, `NewtonianSystem.SatisfiesFirstLaw`,
  `NewtonianSystem.HasLocallyLipschitzForce`, `NewtonianSystem.HasLipschitzForce` and
  `NewtonianSystem.HasC2Potential`: the predicates, with
  `NewtonianSystem.HasLipschitzForce.hasLocallyLipschitzForce` and
  `NewtonianSystem.HasC2Potential.hasLocallyLipschitzForce`.
- `NewtonianSystem.HasLocalSolutions` and `NewtonianSystem.hasLocalSolutions_of_continuous_force`:
  Peano's theorem for Newtonian systems, a continuous force on a finite-dimensional
  configuration space gives local solutions (pending the upstream proof).

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Conservative Newtonian systems
  - A.1. The structure
  - A.2. The force and the equation of motion
  - A.3. Solutions
- B. Determinism and the first law
  - B.1. The properties
  - B.2. Determinism implies the first law
  - B.3. The interval reading of the first law
- C. Regularity conditions
- D. A locally Lipschitz force gives determinism
  - D.1. The phase-space vector field
  - D.2. The phase curve of a solution
  - D.3. The uniqueness theorem
- E. A continuous force gives local solutions
  - E.1. Local existence
  - E.2. The hypotheses of Peano's theorem
  - E.3. The existence theorem

## iv. References

- Earman, J., *A Primer on Determinism*, Reidel (1986).
- Laplace, P.-S., *Essai philosophique sur les probabilités* (1814).
- Montague, R., *Deterministic theories*, in *Formal Philosophy*, Yale University Press (1974).
- Norton, J. D., *The dome: an unexpectedly simple failure of determinism*, Philosophy of
  Science 75 (2008), 786–798.
- `Physlib.ClassicalMechanics.Pendulum.SimplePendulum.Solution` (the same uniqueness argument
  for the pendulum).

sections.text: ## A. Conservative Newtonian systems

### A.1. The structure

The potential is asked to be differentiable and no more, so that the force `-∇V` exists and the
equation of motion can be written pointwise; further regularity is added in section C. Physlib's
general notion is `ClassicalMechanics.PointParticle.NewtonianSystem`, finitely many particles
with explicit forces in a reference frame. The structure here is a single mass in a potential,
which is all the dome needs; the two live in different namespaces and no file opens both.
### A.2. The force and the equation of motion

### A.3. Solutions

A solution is a twice differentiable curve, position and velocity both differentiable, satisfying
the equation of motion: the regularity of `ClassicalMechanics.ReferenceFrame.Particle` and the
least under which the acceleration exists. It is demanded because the pointwise equation, whose
derivatives are zero wherever they do not exist, admits rough accidental solutions. Continuity of
the acceleration is not demanded; for a continuous force it is automatic.
## B. Determinism and the first law

### B.1. The properties

Determinism is the statement that position and velocity at one instant fix the motion at all
instants. The first law, in the reading that says more than the second law, is the statement
that a body at rest where no force acts stays at rest; section B.3 compares the readings. Both
are properties of the system, not of a motion.

The definition of determinism is the naive one. Laplace's formulation is about knowledge; the
notion used since Montague and Earman is about models, a theory being deterministic if any two
models agreeing at one instant agree at every instant. `IsDeterministic` is that notion, with
the models taken to be the twice differentiable solutions of one system, defined for all time,
and the state taken to be position and velocity. Four things follow.

- It is a property of one system. That Newtonian mechanics is deterministic is a claim about
  every system in some class, and which class is what this folder is about.
- It is uniqueness only. A system with no solution from some initial datum, or with solutions
  not defined for all time, counts as deterministic here, whereas on Earman's account such
  failures of existence count against determinism. Existence is kept separate, as
  `HasLocalSolutions`.
- It is relative to the class of solutions. Demanding smooth or analytic solutions would
  exclude the departing motions of the dome, which vanish on a half-line and are not `C⁴`, and
  so restore uniqueness by fiat.
- It does not distinguish future from past. The time-reversed motions of the dome arrive at
  rest on the apex and stay, so the state there fixes neither past nor future; Earman's
  futuristic and historical determinism both fail.

### B.2. Determinism implies the first law

The curve staying at the equilibrium is a solution with the same position and velocity as the
given one at the given instant, so by determinism it is the given one.

### B.3. The interval reading of the first law

The first law can be read instantaneously (no force at an instant, no acceleration then), with
an interval in the hypothesis (no force on an interval, constant velocity on it), or with an
interval in the conclusion (at rest at an instant where no force acts, at rest forever). The
first two follow from the second law for every system, the second being the lemma below, and
both hold for the dome. The third, `SatisfiesFirstLaw`, is determinism at an equilibrium; it is
what the dome violates and what Norton's argument is about, so it is the reading taken here.

## C. Regularity conditions

The hypothesis of the ODE uniqueness theorem is a locally Lipschitz force,
`HasLocallyLipschitzForce`. The two stronger conditions usually stated are a globally Lipschitz
force, `HasLipschitzForce`, and a `C²` potential, `HasC2Potential`, whose force is `C¹`.
Neither implies the other: for example, `x ^ 4` has a `C¹` force of unbounded slope, and
`x * |x| / 2` has the Lipschitz force `-|x|` but is not `C²`. The structure `NewtonianSystem`
of section A assumes none of these conditions; they are separate predicates on it.

## D. A locally Lipschitz force gives determinism

The equation of motion becomes the first-order system `(r, v)' = (v, F(r)/m)` on `X × X`. If
the force is locally Lipschitz so is this vector field, and the local uniqueness theorem
`ODE_solution_unique_of_eventually` of Mathlib, with the connectedness of the real line, gives
determinism, as in `SimplePendulum.equationOfMotion_unique`.
### D.1. The phase-space vector field
### D.2. The phase curve of a solution

### D.3. The uniqueness theorem

Local uniqueness makes the set of instants at which two integral curves through a common point
agree open, continuity makes it closed, and the real line is connected. Applied to the
phase-space vector field this gives the theorem of the file, and sections B, C and D form one
chain, each arrow a theorem:

```
HasC2Potential ────┐
                   ├──▶ HasLocallyLipschitzForce ──▶ IsDeterministic ──▶ SatisfiesFirstLaw
HasLipschitzForce ─┘
```

Naming follows Mathlib: `isDeterministic_of_hasC2Potential` is the arrow from
`HasC2Potential` to `IsDeterministic`.

## E. A continuous force gives local solutions

Determinism is uniqueness; the complementary existence property is that every initial position
and velocity is the initial datum of some solution for a short time. For a continuous force on
a finite-dimensional configuration space this is Peano's theorem applied to the phase-space
vector field, as Picard–Lindelöf gives it for the pendulum in
`SimplePendulum.exists_local_solution`. The statement of Peano's theorem is that of
`NortonDome.PeanoExistence`, pending in Mathlib, so the result here is an informal lemma.
### E.1. Local existence

### E.2. The hypotheses of Peano's theorem

The phase-space vector field is continuous if the force is, and is bounded on the closed unit
ball about the initial datum by compactness; a short enough time interval then gives the
hypotheses of Peano's theorem.

### E.3. The existence theorem

Peano's theorem gives an integral curve through the initial datum, differentiable in the sense
of `HasDerivWithinAt` on the closed interval, hence with an honest derivative on the open one.
Its first component, pulled back to `Time` through `Time.toRealCLE`, is the required curve; its
derivatives are read off with `Time.deriv_comp_toRealCLE_of_hasDerivAt`.

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem
declarations.doc:
A conservative Newtonian system on the configuration space `X`: a point mass `m` in a
differentiable potential `V`. Its equation of motion is Newton's second law `m r̈ = -∇V(r)`.
declarations.statement:
structure NewtonianSystem (X : Type) [NormedAddCommGroup X] [InnerProductSpace ℝ X]
    [CompleteSpace X] where
  /-- The mass. -/
  m : ℝ
  /-- The potential. -/
  potential : X → ℝ
  m_pos : 0 < m
  potential_differentiable : Differentiable ℝ potential

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.m_ne_zero
declarations.doc: The mass of a Newtonian system is not equal to zero.
declarations.statement: lemma m_ne_zero : S.m ≠ 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.force
declarations.doc: The force of a Newtonian system, minus the gradient of the potential.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def force (x : X) : X

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.EquationOfMotion
declarations.doc:
Newton's second law for a Newtonian system: at every instant `m r̈` equals the force at
the position.
declarations.statement: def EquationOfMotion (r : Time → X) : Prop

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.IsSolution
declarations.doc:
A solution of a Newtonian system is a twice differentiable curve, its position and velocity
both differentiable, satisfying the equation of motion.
declarations.statement: def IsSolution (r : Time → X) : Prop

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.IsSolution.differentiable
declarations.doc: The position along a solution is differentiable.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsSolution.differentiable {S : NewtonianSystem X} {r : Time → X} (h : S.IsSolution r) :
    Differentiable ℝ r

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.IsSolution.deriv_differentiable
declarations.doc: The velocity along a solution is differentiable.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsSolution.deriv_differentiable {S : NewtonianSystem X} {r : Time → X}
    (h : S.IsSolution r) : Differentiable ℝ (∂ₜ r)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.IsSolution.equationOfMotion
declarations.doc: A solution satisfies the equation of motion.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsSolution.equationOfMotion {S : NewtonianSystem X} {r : Time → X}
    (h : S.IsSolution r) : S.EquationOfMotion r

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.isSolution_const
declarations.doc: The curve at rest at a point where the force vanishes is a solution.
declarations.statement: lemma isSolution_const {x : X} (hx : S.force x = 0) : S.IsSolution (fun _ => x)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.IsDeterministic
declarations.doc:
A Newtonian system is deterministic if any two solutions with the same position and
velocity at some instant coincide. This is uniqueness of twice differentiable solutions
defined for all time, in both directions of time and without existence; see section B.1.
declarations.statement: def IsDeterministic : Prop

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.SatisfiesFirstLaw
declarations.doc:
A Newtonian system satisfies the first law if a solution at rest, at some instant, at a
point where the force vanishes stays at that point at all instants.
declarations.statement: def SatisfiesFirstLaw : Prop

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.IsDeterministic.satisfiesFirstLaw
declarations.doc: A deterministic Newtonian system satisfies the first law.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsDeterministic.satisfiesFirstLaw {S : NewtonianSystem X} (h : S.IsDeterministic) :
    S.SatisfiesFirstLaw

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.IsSolution.deriv_eq_of_force_eq_zero_on
declarations.doc:
The first law read on an interval: if the force vanishes along a solution throughout the
interval `[a, b]`, the velocity is constant on it. This is a consequence of the second law
alone, and holds for every system.

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.HasLocallyLipschitzForce
declarations.doc:
A Newtonian system has a locally Lipschitz force if its force is Lipschitz on a
neighbourhood of every point. This is the hypothesis of the uniqueness theorem for ordinary
differential equations.
declarations.statement: def HasLocallyLipschitzForce : Prop

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.HasLipschitzForce
declarations.doc: A Newtonian system has a Lipschitz force if its force is globally Lipschitz.
declarations.statement: def HasLipschitzForce : Prop

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.HasC2Potential
declarations.doc:
A Newtonian system has a `C²` potential if its potential is twice continuously
differentiable; two derivatives are what the uniqueness theory of ordinary differential
equations uses.
declarations.statement: def HasC2Potential : Prop

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.HasLipschitzForce.hasLocallyLipschitzForce
declarations.doc: A Lipschitz force is locally Lipschitz.
declarations.statement:
lemma HasLipschitzForce.hasLocallyLipschitzForce (h : S.HasLipschitzForce) :
    S.HasLocallyLipschitzForce

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.HasC2Potential.contDiff_gradient
declarations.doc: The gradient of a `C²` potential is `C¹`.
declarations.statement:

    ContDiff ℝ 1 (gradient S.potential)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.HasC2Potential.hasLocallyLipschitzForce
declarations.doc: The force of a system with a `C²` potential is locally Lipschitz.
declarations.statement:
lemma HasC2Potential.hasLocallyLipschitzForce (h : S.HasC2Potential) :
    S.HasLocallyLipschitzForce

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.phaseVectorField
declarations.doc: The phase-space vector field of a Newtonian system, sending `(r, v)` to `(v, F(r)/m)`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def phaseVectorField (p : X × X) : X × X

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.phaseVectorField_locallyLipschitz
declarations.doc:
If the force of a Newtonian system is locally Lipschitz, so is its phase-space vector
field.
declarations.statement:
lemma phaseVectorField_locallyLipschitz (h : LocallyLipschitz S.force) :
    LocallyLipschitz S.phaseVectorField

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.phaseCurve_hasDerivAt
declarations.doc:
The phase curve `τ ↦ (r t, ṙ t)` (with `t = toRealCLE.symm τ`) of a solution is an
integral curve of the phase-space vector field.
declarations.statement:
lemma phaseCurve_hasDerivAt {r : Time → X} (hr : Differentiable ℝ r)
    (hr' : Differentiable ℝ (∂ₜ r)) (h : S.EquationOfMotion r) (τ : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (fun τ : ℝ => (r (toRealCLE.symm τ), ∂ₜ r (toRealCLE.symm τ)))
      (S.phaseVectorField (r (toRealCLE.symm τ), ∂ₜ r (toRealCLE.symm τ))) τ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.ODE_solution_unique_of_locallyLipschitz
declarations.doc:
Integral curves of a locally Lipschitz vector field, defined at all times, which pass
through the same point at the same instant coincide.
declarations.statement:
lemma ODE_solution_unique_of_locallyLipschitz {E : Type} [NormedAddCommGroup E]
    [NormedSpace ℝ E] {v : E → E} (hv : LocallyLipschitz v) {f g : ℝ → E}
    (hf : ∀ τ, HasDerivAt f (v (f τ)) τ) (hg : ∀ τ, HasDerivAt g (v (g τ)) τ)
    {τ₀ : ℝ} (h0 : f τ₀ = g τ₀) : f = g

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.isDeterministic_of_hasLocallyLipschitzForce
declarations.doc:
The uniqueness theorem for Newtonian systems: a Newtonian system with a locally Lipschitz
force is deterministic.
declarations.statement:
lemma isDeterministic_of_hasLocallyLipschitzForce (h : S.HasLocallyLipschitzForce) :
    S.IsDeterministic

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.isDeterministic_of_hasLipschitzForce
declarations.doc:
Picard–Lindelöf for Newtonian systems: a Newtonian system with a Lipschitz force is
deterministic.
declarations.statement: lemma isDeterministic_of_hasLipschitzForce (h : S.HasLipschitzForce) : S.IsDeterministic

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.isDeterministic_of_hasC2Potential
declarations.doc: A Newtonian system with a `C²` potential is deterministic.
declarations.statement: lemma isDeterministic_of_hasC2Potential (h : S.HasC2Potential) : S.IsDeterministic

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.satisfiesFirstLaw_of_hasLocallyLipschitzForce
declarations.doc: A Newtonian system with a locally Lipschitz force satisfies the first law.
declarations.statement:
lemma satisfiesFirstLaw_of_hasLocallyLipschitzForce (h : S.HasLocallyLipschitzForce) :
    S.SatisfiesFirstLaw

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.HasLocalSolutions
declarations.doc:
A Newtonian system has local solutions if for every initial position `x₀` and velocity
`v₀` there are `ε > 0` and a curve `r` with `r 0 = x₀` and `ṙ 0 = v₀` which, at every time
within `ε` of the initial instant, is differentiable together with its velocity and satisfies
the equation of motion.
declarations.statement: def HasLocalSolutions : Prop

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.phaseVectorField_continuous
declarations.doc: If the force of a Newtonian system is continuous, so is its phase-space vector field.
declarations.statement:
lemma phaseVectorField_continuous (hF : Continuous S.force) :
    Continuous S.phaseVectorField

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NewtonianSystem.exists_isPeano_phaseVectorField
declarations.doc:
For a continuous force on a finite-dimensional configuration space, the time-independent
phase-space vector field satisfies the hypotheses of Peano's theorem about any initial datum,
on a short enough symmetric time interval and the closed unit ball.
declarations.statement:
lemma exists_isPeano_phaseVectorField [FiniteDimensional ℝ X] (hF : Continuous S.force)
    (p₀ : X × X) :
    ∃ δ > (0 : ℝ), ∃ L : NNReal,
      IsPeano (fun q : ℝ × (X × X) => S.phaseVectorField q.2) (-δ) δ 0 p₀ 1 L

modules.title: Peano's existence theorem (statements)
modules.doc:
Statements of Peano's existence theorem for ODEs, pending its proof in Mathlib.

## i. Overview

Peano's existence theorem: the initial value problem `x' = f (t, x)`, `x t₀ = x₀` has a
solution on a closed time interval whenever `f` is continuous on the product of that interval
with a closed ball about `x₀` and the interval is short enough for the solution to stay in the
ball. No Lipschitz condition is asked, and only existence is guaranteed.

The theorem is not yet in Mathlib. This file records the hypotheses and the two forms of the
conclusion as stated in the Mathlib pull request
[#42148](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/42148), by Julian Rolfes,
Luke Schleef, Philipp Svinger, Paul Niessner and Florian Grube, as
informal lemmas. Names and namespace are those of the pull
request, so that once it is merged this file can be deleted and its uses redirected to
Mathlib's `IsPeano` by a change of imports. `NortonDome.NewtonianSystem` uses the theorem to
show that a Newtonian system with a continuous force has local solutions.

## ii. Key results

- `IsPeano` collects the hypotheses: the initial time lies in the interval, the vector field is
  continuous on the cylinder, bounded by `L` there, and `L` times the length of the interval on
  either side of `t₀` is at most the radius `r` of the ball.
- `IsPeano.exists_eq_forall_mem_Icc_eq_integral` is the theorem in integral form.
- `IsPeano.exists_eq_forall_mem_Icc_hasDerivWithinAt₀` is the theorem in differential form.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The hypotheses
- B. The theorem

## iv. References

- Mathlib pull request [#42148](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/42148),
  `Mathlib/Analysis/ODE/Peano.lean`.
- Hartman, P., *Ordinary Differential Equations*, 2nd ed., SIAM (2002), Theorem II.2.1.

sections.text: ## A. The hypotheses
## B. The theorem

declarations.name: IsPeano
declarations.doc: The hypotheses for Peano's existence theorem on a closed time interval and a closed ball.
declarations.statement:
structure IsPeano {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E]
    (f : ℝ × E → E) (tmin tmax t₀ : ℝ) (x₀ : E) (r L : ℝ≥0) : Prop where
  /-- The initial time belongs to the time interval. -/
  t₀_mem : t₀ ∈ Icc tmin tmax
  /-- The vector field is continuous on the set product of a time interval and a closed ball. -/
  continuousOn : ContinuousOn f (Icc tmin tmax ×ˢ closedBall x₀ r)
  /-- `L` is an upper bound of the norm of the vector field. -/
  norm_le : ∀ t ∈ Icc tmin tmax, ∀ x ∈ closedBall x₀ r, ‖f (t, x)‖ ≤ L
  /-- The time interval of validity. -/
  mul_max_le : L * max (tmax - t₀) (t₀ - tmin) ≤ r

modules.title: The Norton dome in physical space
modules.doc:
The Norton dome chart dynamics as a point mass constrained to the dome surface.

## i. Overview

`NortonDome.Basic` writes the dynamics on the arc length `r`, with kinetic energy `½ m ṙ²` and
potential energy `-m g h(r)`. This module identifies that chart dynamics with a point mass
constrained to the surface of the dome, as `SimplePendulum.Geometric.PhysicalSpace` does for
the pendulum.

The motion is radial, so it suffices to work in the vertical plane through the apex, with the
apex at the origin and the vertical coordinate measured upwards. The profile is the arc-length
parametrised curve `s ↦ (x(s), -h(s))`, where `x'(s)² + h'(s)² = 1` and `h'(s) = √s / g` give
`x'(s) = √(1 - s/g²)` and `x(s) = (2g²/3) (1 - (1 - s/g²)^{3/2})`. The profile exists for
`0 ≤ s ≤ g²`; at `s = g²` it is vertical and Norton's model stops. While the arc length is in
that range the chart kinetic energy is `½ m ‖v‖²` by unit speed, and the chart potential energy
is the gravitational potential `m g y` at height `y`, so the chart Lagrangian is the
constrained Lagrangian.

## ii. Key results

- `NortonDome.horizontal` is the horizontal distance `x(s)` of the profile from the apex, with
  its derivative `hasDerivAt_horizontal`; `NortonDome.unit_speed` is the identity
  `x'(s)² + h'(s)² = 1`.
- `NortonDome.profile` is the profile curve `s ↦ (x(s), -h(s))` in the vertical plane, and
  `NortonDome.dome` its image on `0 ≤ s ≤ g²`.
- `NortonDome.spaceTrajectory` is the position of the particle in the plane along a chart
  trajectory; it lies on the dome, `spaceTrajectory_mem_dome`, while the arc length is in range.
- `NortonDome.deriv_spaceTrajectory` is the velocity of the particle in the plane, with the
  square of its speed `norm_sq_deriv_spaceTrajectory`.
- `NortonDome.kineticEnergy_eq_space`, `NortonDome.potentialEnergy_eq_height`,
  `NortonDome.lagrangian_eq_space` and `NortonDome.energy_eq_space` identify the chart
  energies and Lagrangian with those of the point mass in physical space.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The profile of the dome in the plane
  - A.1. The horizontal coordinate and the unit-speed property
  - A.2. The profile curve and the dome
- B. The particle's position along a trajectory
- C. The particle's velocity and speed
- D. The energies and the Lagrangian in physical space

## iv. References

- Norton, J. D., *The dome: an unexpectedly simple failure of determinism*, Philosophy of
  Science 75 (2008), 786–798.
- `Physlib.ClassicalMechanics.Pendulum.SimplePendulum.Geometric.PhysicalSpace` (the same
  identification for the pendulum).

sections.text: ## A. The profile of the dome in the plane

### A.1. The horizontal coordinate and the unit-speed property

The horizontal distance from the apex has derivative `√(1 - s/g²)`; with the slope `√s / g` of
the depth this gives unit speed.
### A.2. The profile curve and the dome

## B. The particle's position along a trajectory

Along a chart trajectory `r` the particle is at the point of the profile at arc length
`r t 0`, on the dome while that is in range.

## C. The particle's velocity and speed

The velocity in the plane is the unit tangent `(x'(r), -h'(r))` times `ṙ`, so by unit speed the
square of the speed is `ṙ²` while the arc length is in range.

## D. The energies and the Lagrangian in physical space

The chart kinetic energy is that of the particle in the plane while the arc length is in range,
and the chart potential energy is `m g y` at its height `y` at all times; the chart Lagrangian
is the constrained Lagrangian `T - V`.

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.horizontal
declarations.doc:
The horizontal distance `x(s) = (2g²/3) (1 - (1 - s/g²)^{3/2})` of the profile of the dome
from the apex at arc length `s`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def horizontal (s : ℝ) : ℝ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.horizontal_eq
declarations.doc: The horizontal distance of the profile from the apex, written out.
declarations.statement:
lemma horizontal_eq (s : ℝ) :
    S.horizontal s = 2 * S.g ^ 2 / 3 * (1 - √(1 - s / S.g ^ 2) ^ 3)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.horizontal_zero
declarations.doc: The profile of the dome starts at the apex.
declarations.statement: lemma horizontal_zero : S.horizontal 0 = 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.hasDerivAt_horizontal
declarations.doc:
The derivative of the horizontal distance with respect to the arc length is `√(1 - s/g²)`,
at every `s`.
declarations.statement: lemma hasDerivAt_horizontal (s : ℝ) : HasDerivAt S.horizontal (√(1 - s / S.g ^ 2)) s

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.horizontal_differentiable
declarations.doc:
The horizontal distance of the profile from the apex is a differentiable function of the
arc length.
declarations.statement: lemma horizontal_differentiable : Differentiable ℝ S.horizontal

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.unit_speed
declarations.doc:
Unit speed: for arc length `0 ≤ s ≤ g²` the derivatives of the horizontal distance and
of the depth satisfy `x'(s)² + h'(s)² = 1`, so that `s` is indeed the arc length along the
profile.
declarations.statement:
lemma unit_speed {s : ℝ} (h0 : 0 ≤ s) (h1 : s ≤ S.g ^ 2) :
    √(1 - s / S.g ^ 2) ^ 2 + (√s / S.g) ^ 2 = 1

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.profile
declarations.doc:
The profile of the dome in the vertical plane through the apex: the point at arc length
`s` is at horizontal distance `x(s)` from the apex and at height `-h(s)`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def profile (s : ℝ) : Space 2

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.profile_apply_zero
declarations.doc: The horizontal coordinate of the profile of the dome.
declarations.statement: lemma profile_apply_zero (s : ℝ) : S.profile s 0 = S.horizontal s

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.profile_apply_one
declarations.doc: The vertical coordinate of the profile of the dome is minus its depth below the apex.
declarations.statement: lemma profile_apply_one (s : ℝ) : S.profile s 1 = -S.height s

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.profile_zero
declarations.doc: The apex of the dome is the origin.
declarations.statement: lemma profile_zero : S.profile 0 = 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.dome
declarations.doc:
The dome, in the vertical plane through its apex: the image of the profile on the range
`0 ≤ s ≤ g²` of arc lengths on which the profile exists.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def dome : Set (Space 2)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.profile_mem_dome
declarations.doc: The point of the profile at arc length `0 ≤ s ≤ g²` lies on the dome.
declarations.statement: lemma profile_mem_dome {s : ℝ} (h0 : 0 ≤ s) (h1 : s ≤ S.g ^ 2) : S.profile s ∈ S.dome

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.spaceTrajectory
declarations.doc:
The position of the particle in the plane along the chart trajectory `r` of the arc
length.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def spaceTrajectory (r : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) : Time → Space 2

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.spaceTrajectory_apply_zero
declarations.doc: The horizontal position of the particle along a chart trajectory.
declarations.statement:
lemma spaceTrajectory_apply_zero (r : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) (t : Time) :
    S.spaceTrajectory r t 0 = S.horizontal (r t 0)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.spaceTrajectory_apply_one
declarations.doc:
The height of the particle along a chart trajectory is minus the depth of the dome at its
arc length.
declarations.statement:
lemma spaceTrajectory_apply_one (r : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) (t : Time) :
    S.spaceTrajectory r t 1 = -S.height (r t 0)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.spaceTrajectory_mem_dome
declarations.doc: While its arc length is in the range `0 ≤ r ≤ g²` the particle is on the dome.
declarations.statement:
lemma spaceTrajectory_mem_dome (r : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) {t : Time}
    (h0 : 0 ≤ r t 0) (h1 : r t 0 ≤ S.g ^ 2) : S.spaceTrajectory r t ∈ S.dome

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.differentiable_spaceTrajectory
declarations.doc:
Along a differentiable chart trajectory the position of the particle is differentiable in
time.
declarations.statement:
lemma differentiable_spaceTrajectory (r : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1))
    (hr : Differentiable ℝ r) : Differentiable ℝ (S.spaceTrajectory r)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.deriv_spaceTrajectory
declarations.doc:
The velocity of the particle in the plane along a differentiable chart trajectory `r` is
`(√(1 - r/g²), -√r / g)` times the rate of change `ṙ` of the arc length: the unit tangent
vector to the profile times `ṙ`.
declarations.statement:
lemma deriv_spaceTrajectory (r : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) (hr : Differentiable ℝ r)
    (t : Time) :
    ∂ₜᵥ (S.spaceTrajectory r) t =
      !₂[√(1 - r t 0 / S.g ^ 2) * (∂ₜ r t) 0, -(√(r t 0) / S.g) * (∂ₜ r t) 0]

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.norm_sq_deriv_spaceTrajectory
declarations.doc:
While the arc length is in range, the square of the speed of the particle along a
differentiable chart trajectory is `ṙ²`.
declarations.statement:
lemma norm_sq_deriv_spaceTrajectory (r : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1))
    (hr : Differentiable ℝ r) {t : Time} (h0 : 0 ≤ r t 0) (h1 : r t 0 ≤ S.g ^ 2) :
    ‖∂ₜᵥ (S.spaceTrajectory r) t‖ ^ 2 = ((∂ₜ r t) 0) ^ 2

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.kineticEnergy_eq_space
declarations.doc:
The chart kinetic energy of the dome along a differentiable chart trajectory is the kinetic
energy of the particle in physical space, while the arc length is in range.
declarations.statement:
lemma kineticEnergy_eq_space (r : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) (hr : Differentiable ℝ r)
    {t : Time} (h0 : 0 ≤ r t 0) (h1 : r t 0 ≤ S.g ^ 2) :
    S.kineticEnergy r t = (1 / (2 : ℝ)) * S.m * ‖∂ₜᵥ (S.spaceTrajectory r) t‖ ^ 2

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.potentialEnergy_eq_height
declarations.doc:
The chart potential energy of the dome is the gravitational potential `m g y` of the
particle at its height `y` in physical space.
declarations.statement:
lemma potentialEnergy_eq_height (r : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) (t : Time) :
    S.potentialEnergy (r t) = S.m * S.g * S.spaceTrajectory r t 1

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.lagrangian_eq_space
declarations.doc:
The chart Lagrangian of the dome along a differentiable chart trajectory is the constrained
Lagrangian of the particle in physical space, while the arc length is in range.
declarations.statement:
lemma lagrangian_eq_space (r : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) (hr : Differentiable ℝ r)
    {t : Time} (h0 : 0 ≤ r t 0) (h1 : r t 0 ≤ S.g ^ 2) :
    S.lagrangian t (r t) (∂ₜ r t) =
      (1 / (2 : ℝ)) * S.m * ‖∂ₜᵥ (S.spaceTrajectory r) t‖ ^ 2
        - S.m * S.g * S.spaceTrajectory r t 1

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.energy_eq_space
declarations.doc:
The chart energy of the dome along a differentiable chart trajectory is the total energy of
the particle in physical space, while the arc length is in range.
declarations.statement:
lemma energy_eq_space (r : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) (hr : Differentiable ℝ r)
    {t : Time} (h0 : 0 ≤ r t 0) (h1 : r t 0 ≤ S.g ^ 2) :
    S.energy r t =
      (1 / (2 : ℝ)) * S.m * ‖∂ₜᵥ (S.spaceTrajectory r) t‖ ^ 2
        + S.m * S.g * S.spaceTrajectory r t 1

modules.title: Powers of the positive part
modules.doc:
The derivative and `C^(n+1)` regularity of `y ↦ max (y - c) 0 ^ (n + 2)`.

## i. Overview

The function `y ↦ max (y - c) 0 ^ (n + 2)` vanishes to the left of `c` and is a polynomial to
its right. It is differentiable everywhere, including at `c`, and is `C^(n+1)`. Functions of
this shape are the standard witnesses for the failure of uniqueness of ODEs with a
non-Lipschitz right-hand side, of which the Norton dome is the physical instance.

## ii. Key results

- `hasDerivAt_max_sub_pow` is the derivative `(n + 2) max (y - c) 0 ^ (n + 1)`, at every point.
- `contDiff_max_sub_pow` is the `C^(n+1)` regularity.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The derivative
- B. Regularity

## iv. References

- Norton, J. D., *The dome: an unexpectedly simple failure of determinism*, Philosophy of
  Science 75 (2008), 786–798.

sections.text:
## A. The derivative

By cases: to the left of `c` the function vanishes near the point, to the right it agrees near
the point with `(y - c) ^ (n + 2)`, and at `c` the difference quotient is `max t 0 ^ (n + 1)`,
which tends to zero.

## B. Regularity

By induction on `n`: the derivative of the `(n + 3)`-rd power is a constant multiple of the
`(n + 2)`-nd, which is `C^(n+1)` by the induction hypothesis.

declarations.name: hasDerivAt_max_sub_pow
declarations.doc:
The power `max (y - c) 0 ^ (n + 2)` of the positive part of `y - c` has derivative
`(n + 2) max (x - c) 0 ^ (n + 1)` at every `x`, including the junction `x = c`.
declarations.statement:
lemma hasDerivAt_max_sub_pow (c : ℝ) (n : ℕ) (x : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (fun y : ℝ => max (y - c) 0 ^ (n + 2))
      (((n : ℝ) + 2) * max (x - c) 0 ^ (n + 1)) x

declarations.name: contDiff_max_sub_pow
declarations.doc: The power `max (y - c) 0 ^ (n + 2)` of the positive part of `y - c` is `C^(n+1)`.
declarations.statement:
lemma contDiff_max_sub_pow (c : ℝ) (n : ℕ) :
    ContDiff ℝ (n + 1) (fun y : ℝ => max (y - c) 0 ^ (n + 2))

modules.title: The motions of the Norton dome and the failure of uniqueness
modules.doc:
The Norton dome has infinitely many motions from rest at its apex: uniqueness fails.

## i. Overview

A particle at rest on the apex of the Norton dome satisfies `r̈ = √r` by staying there forever,
and also by staying until an arbitrary instant `T ≥ 0` and then sliding off along
`r(t) = (t - T)⁴ / 144`: that curve is `C²`, vanishes with its derivative at `T`, and its
second derivative `(t - T)² / 12` is `√r`. All these motions have the same initial position and
velocity, so the initial data do not determine the motion. This is Norton's observation.

For contrast, the pendulum's phase-space vector field is Lipschitz and Mathlib's
`ODE_solution_unique_univ` gives `SimplePendulum.equationOfMotion_unique`; the force of the
dome is not Lipschitz at the apex, `NortonDome.not_lipschitzOnWith_force`. Energy conservation
does not help either, since every motion in the family has zero energy (`energy_solution`).
Read backwards in time, in section E, a particle sliding up the dome may arrive at the apex at
rest in finite time and stay there.

## ii. Key results

- `NortonDome.delayedQuartic` is the real function `τ ↦ max (τ - T) 0 ⁴ / 144`, with its
  derivatives `hasDerivAt_delayedQuartic` and `hasDerivAt_deriv_delayedQuartic`, its `C²`
  regularity `contDiff_delayedQuartic`, and the identity `sqrt_delayedQuartic`.
- `NortonDome.solution T` is the motion leaving the apex at the instant `T`. It is a solution,
  `solution_isSolution`, starts from rest at the apex when `0 ≤ T`, `solution_zero` and
  `deriv_solution_zero`, and is injective in `T`, `solution_injective`.
- `NortonDome.rest_isSolution` is the motion staying at the apex.
- `NortonDome.exists_isSolution_ne` is the failure of uniqueness: two distinct solutions with
  the same initial position and velocity; `NortonDome.not_isSolution_unique` restates it as
  the negation of the uniqueness property of the pendulum. All these motions have zero energy,
  `NortonDome.energy_rest` and `NortonDome.energy_solution`.
- `NortonDome.IsSolution.comp_neg` is the time-reversal symmetry of the dome, and
  `NortonDome.arrival T` the time-reversed motion, off the apex before the instant `-T`,
  `arrival_apply_pos`, and at rest on it from then on, `arrival_of_le`.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The delayed quartic
  - A.1. Definition and sign
  - A.2. Derivatives and regularity
- B. The motions leaving the apex
  - B.1. The definition and its values
  - B.2. Derivatives and regularity
  - B.3. The equation of motion
  - B.4. Distinct instants give distinct motions
- C. The motion staying at the apex
- D. The failure of uniqueness
- E. Time reversal and arrival at the apex

## iv. References

- Norton, J. D., *The dome: an unexpectedly simple failure of determinism*, Philosophy of
  Science 75 (2008), 786–798.
- `Physlib.ClassicalMechanics.Pendulum.SimplePendulum.Solution` (uniqueness for a Lipschitz
  force, for contrast).

sections.text:
## A. The delayed quartic

As a function of the real time `τ`, the motion leaving the apex at the instant `T` is
`max (τ - T) 0 ⁴ / 144`; its calculus is that of the positive-part powers of
`NortonDome.PosPartPow`.
### A.1. Definition and sign
### A.2. Derivatives and regularity

## B. The motions leaving the apex

The motion leaving the apex at the instant `T` is the delayed quartic read on `Time`, times the
unit vector of the arc-length coordinate.
### B.1. The definition and its values
### B.2. Derivatives and regularity
### B.3. The equation of motion
### B.4. Distinct instants give distinct motions

## C. The motion staying at the apex

The force vanishes at the apex, so the constant curve there satisfies the equation of motion.

## D. The failure of uniqueness

Rest at the apex and departure at any instant `T ≥ 0` are distinct solutions with the same
initial data. So the uniqueness property `SimplePendulum.IsSolution.eq_of_initial` of the
pendulum fails for the dome, whose force violates the Picard–Lindelöf hypothesis
(`not_lipschitzOnWith_force`).

## E. Time reversal and arrival at the apex

The equation of motion has no velocity term, so time reversal maps solutions to solutions.
Reversing the departure at the instant `T` gives a motion sliding up the dome, arriving at the
apex at the instant `-T` with zero velocity, and staying there. For a locally Lipschitz force
this is impossible; for the dome it is the non-uniqueness read backwards.

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.delayedQuartic
declarations.doc:
The delayed quartic `τ ↦ max (τ - T) 0 ⁴ / 144`: zero up to the instant `T`, and
`(τ - T)⁴ / 144` afterwards.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def delayedQuartic (T τ : ℝ) : ℝ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.delayedQuartic_eq
declarations.doc: The delayed quartic, written out.
declarations.statement: lemma delayedQuartic_eq (T τ : ℝ) : delayedQuartic T τ = max (τ - T) 0 ^ 4 / 144

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.delayedQuartic_nonneg
declarations.doc: The delayed quartic is non-negative.
declarations.statement: lemma delayedQuartic_nonneg (T τ : ℝ) : 0 ≤ delayedQuartic T τ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.delayedQuartic_of_le
declarations.doc: The delayed quartic vanishes up to the instant `T`.
declarations.statement: lemma delayedQuartic_of_le (T : ℝ) {τ : ℝ} (h : τ ≤ T) : delayedQuartic T τ = 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.delayedQuartic_pos
declarations.doc: The delayed quartic is positive after the instant `T`.
declarations.statement: lemma delayedQuartic_pos (T : ℝ) {τ : ℝ} (h : T < τ) : 0 < delayedQuartic T τ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.sqrt_delayedQuartic
declarations.doc:
The square root of the delayed quartic is `max (τ - T) 0 ² / 12`, which is its second
derivative: this is the equation of motion `r̈ = √r` of the dome along it.
declarations.statement: lemma sqrt_delayedQuartic (T τ : ℝ) : √(delayedQuartic T τ) = max (τ - T) 0 ^ 2 / 12

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.hasDerivAt_delayedQuartic
declarations.doc: The derivative of the delayed quartic is `max (τ - T) 0 ³ / 36`.
declarations.statement:
lemma hasDerivAt_delayedQuartic (T τ : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (delayedQuartic T) (max (τ - T) 0 ^ 3 / 36) τ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.deriv_delayedQuartic
declarations.doc: The derivative of the delayed quartic, as a function.
declarations.statement:
lemma deriv_delayedQuartic (T : ℝ) :
    deriv (delayedQuartic T) = fun τ => max (τ - T) 0 ^ 3 / 36

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.hasDerivAt_deriv_delayedQuartic
declarations.doc: The second derivative of the delayed quartic is `max (τ - T) 0 ² / 12`.
declarations.statement:
lemma hasDerivAt_deriv_delayedQuartic (T τ : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (deriv (delayedQuartic T)) (max (τ - T) 0 ^ 2 / 12) τ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.contDiff_delayedQuartic
declarations.doc: The delayed quartic is `C²`. It is in fact `C³` and not `C⁴`, which is not needed here.
declarations.statement: lemma contDiff_delayedQuartic (T : ℝ) : ContDiff ℝ 2 (delayedQuartic T)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.solution
declarations.doc:
The motion of the particle on the dome leaving the apex at the instant `T`: at rest at the
apex up to `T`, and at arc length `(t - T)⁴ / 144` from the apex afterwards.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def solution (T : ℝ) : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.solution_apply
declarations.doc:
The arc length along the motion leaving the apex at the instant `T` is the delayed
quartic.
declarations.statement: lemma solution_apply (T : ℝ) (t : Time) : solution T t 0 = delayedQuartic T t.val

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.solution_of_le
declarations.doc: The motion leaving the apex at the instant `T` is at the apex up to `T`.
declarations.statement: lemma solution_of_le (T : ℝ) {t : Time} (h : t.val ≤ T) : solution T t = 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.solution_zero
declarations.doc: The motion leaving the apex at the instant `T ≥ 0` starts at the apex.
declarations.statement: lemma solution_zero {T : ℝ} (hT : 0 ≤ T) : solution T 0 = 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.solution_apply_pos
declarations.doc: The motion leaving the apex at the instant `T` is off the apex after `T`.
declarations.statement: lemma solution_apply_pos (T : ℝ) {t : Time} (h : T < t.val) : 0 < solution T t 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.solution_contDiff
declarations.doc: The motion leaving the apex at the instant `T` is `C²`.
declarations.statement: lemma solution_contDiff (T : ℝ) : ContDiff ℝ 2 (solution T)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.deriv_solution
declarations.doc:
The velocity along the motion leaving the apex at the instant `T` is
`max (t - T) 0 ³ / 36`.
declarations.statement:
lemma deriv_solution (T : ℝ) :
    ∂ₜ (solution T) = fun t => (max (t.val - T) 0 ^ 3 / 36) • EuclideanSpace.single 0 1

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.deriv_deriv_solution
declarations.doc:
The acceleration along the motion leaving the apex at the instant `T` is
`max (t - T) 0 ² / 12`.
declarations.statement:
lemma deriv_deriv_solution (T : ℝ) :
    ∂ₜ (∂ₜ (solution T)) =
      fun t => (max (t.val - T) 0 ^ 2 / 12) • EuclideanSpace.single 0 1

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.deriv_solution_zero
declarations.doc: The motion leaving the apex at the instant `T ≥ 0` starts from rest.
declarations.statement: lemma deriv_solution_zero {T : ℝ} (hT : 0 ≤ T) : ∂ₜ (solution T) 0 = 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.solution_equationOfMotion
declarations.doc:
The motion leaving the apex at the instant `T` satisfies the equation of motion of the
dome: its acceleration `max (t - T) 0 ² / 12` is the square root of its arc length.
declarations.statement: lemma solution_equationOfMotion (T : ℝ) : S.EquationOfMotion (solution T)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.solution_isSolution
declarations.doc: The motion leaving the apex at the instant `T` is a solution of the dome.
declarations.statement: lemma solution_isSolution (T : ℝ) : S.IsSolution (solution T)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.solution_ne_of_lt
declarations.doc:
Motions leaving the apex at distinct instants are distinct: at the later instant one is
still at the apex and the other is not.
declarations.statement: lemma solution_ne_of_lt {T T' : ℝ} (h : T < T') : solution T ≠ solution T'

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.solution_injective
declarations.doc: The family of motions leaving the apex is injective in the instant of departure.
declarations.statement: lemma solution_injective : Function.Injective solution

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.solution_ne_zero
declarations.doc: No motion leaving the apex is the motion staying at it.
declarations.statement: lemma solution_ne_zero (T : ℝ) : solution T ≠ 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.rest_isSolution
declarations.doc: The motion staying at rest at the apex is a solution of the dome.
declarations.statement: lemma rest_isSolution : S.IsSolution 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.energy_rest
declarations.doc: The motion staying at the apex has zero energy.
declarations.statement: lemma energy_rest (t : Time) : S.energy 0 t = 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.exists_isSolution_ne
declarations.doc:
Failure of uniqueness for the Norton dome: there are two distinct solutions of the
dome with the same initial position and the same initial velocity. The witnesses are the
motion staying at the apex and the motion leaving it at the instant `0`.
declarations.statement:
lemma exists_isSolution_ne :
    ∃ x y : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1), S.IsSolution x ∧ S.IsSolution y ∧
      x 0 = y 0 ∧ ∂ₜ x 0 = ∂ₜ y 0 ∧ x ≠ y

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.not_isSolution_unique
declarations.doc:
The solutions of the Norton dome are not determined by their initial position and
velocity: the uniqueness property that the simple pendulum has,
`SimplePendulum.IsSolution.eq_of_initial`, fails for the dome.
declarations.statement:
lemma not_isSolution_unique :
    ¬ ∀ x y : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1), S.IsSolution x → S.IsSolution y →
      x 0 = y 0 → ∂ₜ x 0 = ∂ₜ y 0 → x = y

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.exists_isSolution_of_nonneg
declarations.doc:
For every instant `T ≥ 0` there is a solution of the dome starting from rest at the apex
which is at the apex up to `T` and off it afterwards: the motions from rest at the apex form
a one-parameter family.
declarations.statement:
lemma exists_isSolution_of_nonneg {T : ℝ} (hT : 0 ≤ T) :
    ∃ r : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1), S.IsSolution r ∧ r 0 = 0 ∧ ∂ₜ r 0 = 0 ∧
      (∀ t : Time, t.val ≤ T → r t = 0) ∧ (∀ t : Time, T < t.val → 0 < r t 0)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.energy_solution
declarations.doc:
Every motion leaving the apex has zero energy: before the instant `T` it is at rest at the
apex, and the energy is conserved. Energy conservation therefore does not single out the
motion staying at the apex.
declarations.statement: lemma energy_solution (T : ℝ) (t : Time) : S.energy (solution T) t = 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.deriv_deriv_comp_neg_of_differentiable
declarations.doc:
The second derivative is unchanged by the reversal of time, for a curve whose position and
velocity are differentiable. This is `Time.deriv_deriv_comp_neg` with its `C²` hypothesis
weakened to the regularity of a solution.
declarations.statement:
lemma deriv_deriv_comp_neg_of_differentiable {M : Type} [NormedAddCommGroup M]
    [NormedSpace ℝ M] (f : Time → M) (hf : Differentiable ℝ f) (hf' : Differentiable ℝ (∂ₜ f))
    (t : Time) : ∂ₜ (∂ₜ (fun s => f (-s))) t = ∂ₜ (∂ₜ f) (-t)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.equationOfMotion_comp_neg
declarations.doc:
The time reversal of a twice differentiable curve satisfying the equation of motion of the
dome satisfies it too: the equation has no velocity term.
declarations.statement:
lemma equationOfMotion_comp_neg {r : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)} (hr : Differentiable ℝ r)
    (hr' : Differentiable ℝ (∂ₜ r)) (h : S.EquationOfMotion r) :
    S.EquationOfMotion (fun t => r (-t))

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.IsSolution.comp_neg
declarations.doc: The time reversal of a solution of the dome is a solution.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsSolution.comp_neg {S : NortonDome} {r : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)}
    (h : S.IsSolution r) : S.IsSolution (fun t => r (-t))

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.arrival
declarations.doc:
The motion of the particle on the dome arriving at the apex at the instant `-T`: the time
reversal of the motion leaving the apex at the instant `T`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def arrival (T : ℝ) : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.arrival_isSolution
declarations.doc: The motion arriving at the apex at the instant `-T` is a solution of the dome.
declarations.statement: lemma arrival_isSolution (T : ℝ) : S.IsSolution (arrival T)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.arrival_apply_pos
declarations.doc:
The motion arriving at the apex at the instant `-T` is off the apex before that
instant.
declarations.statement: lemma arrival_apply_pos (T : ℝ) {t : Time} (h : t.val < -T) : 0 < arrival T t 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.arrival_of_le
declarations.doc:
The motion arriving at the apex at the instant `-T` is at the apex from that instant on:
it reaches the apex in finite time and stays there.
declarations.statement: lemma arrival_of_le (T : ℝ) {t : Time} (h : -T ≤ t.val) : arrival T t = 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.NortonDome.deriv_arrival_of_le
declarations.doc: The motion arriving at the apex at the instant `-T` arrives with zero velocity.
declarations.statement: lemma deriv_arrival_of_le (T : ℝ) {t : Time} (h : -T ≤ t.val) : ∂ₜ (arrival T) t = 0

modules.title: Calculus of the real square root near zero
modules.doc:
The derivative of `√y ^ 3` everywhere, and the failure of the Lipschitz property of `√` at 0.

## i. Overview

Two facts about the real square root at zero, where Mathlib's calculus does not reach: the
cube `√y ^ 3` is differentiable everywhere, with derivative `(3/2) √x`, and `√` is not
Lipschitz on any interval `[0, ε]`. The first gives the derivative of the potential of the
Norton dome, the second the failure of the Picard–Lindelöf hypothesis for its force.

## ii. Key results

- `hasDerivAt_sqrt_pow_three` is the derivative of `√y ^ 3` at every real number.
- `not_lipschitzOnWith_sqrt` is the failure of the Lipschitz property of `√` on `[0, ε]`.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The derivative of the cube of the square root
- B. The square root is not Lipschitz at zero

## iv. References

- Norton, J. D., *The dome: an unexpectedly simple failure of determinism*, Philosophy of
  Science 75 (2008), 786–798.

sections.text:
## A. The derivative of the cube of the square root

To the left of zero the square root vanishes, to the right the chain rule applies, and at zero
the difference quotient of `√t ^ 3 = t √t` is `√t`, which tends to zero.

## B. The square root is not Lipschitz at zero

A bound `√y ≤ K y` on `[0, ε]` gives `1 ≤ K √y` for every positive `y ≤ ε`, which fails at
`y = min ε (1 / (2K + 1)²)`.

declarations.name: hasDerivAt_sqrt_pow_three
declarations.doc:
The cube of the real square root, `√y ^ 3`, has derivative `(3/2) √x` at every real `x`. It
is differentiable at `0`, with derivative `0`, even though `√` is not.
declarations.statement:
lemma hasDerivAt_sqrt_pow_three (x : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (fun y : ℝ => √y ^ 3) (3 / 2 * √x) x

declarations.name: not_lipschitzOnWith_sqrt
declarations.doc:
The real square root is not Lipschitz on any interval `[0, ε]` with `ε > 0`, for any
Lipschitz constant.
declarations.statement:
lemma not_lipschitzOnWith_sqrt (K : NNReal) {ε : ℝ} (hε : 0 < ε) :
    ¬ LipschitzOnWith K (fun y : ℝ => √y) (Set.Icc 0 ε)

modules.title: Circular orbits for the Hohmann transfer
modules.doc:
The two circular coasts obey the same central force law.

## i. Overview

A circular orbit rotates uniformly at the rate determined by the radius and gravitational
parameter. The phase is free so its position can meet the transfer ellipse at an apsis.

## ii. Key results

- `circular_newton` gives the main result of this module.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Circular positions, velocities, and accelerations

## iv. References

- [ref: hohmann_jpl_orbital_mechanics] describes the Hohmann ellipse and its apses.

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.circularSpeed

declarations.statement: def circularVelocity (mu R phase t : ℝ) : ℂ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.circularRate_pos
declarations.statement:
lemma circularRate_pos {mu R : ℝ} (hm : 0 < mu) (hR : 0 < R) :
    0 < circularRate mu R

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.circularRate_sq
declarations.statement:
lemma circularRate_sq {mu R : ℝ} (hm : 0 < mu) (hR : 0 < R) :
    circularRate mu R ^ 2 = mu/R^3

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.circularSpeed_pos
declarations.statement:
lemma circularSpeed_pos {mu R : ℝ} (hm : 0 < mu) (hR : 0 < R) :
    0 < circularSpeed mu R

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.circularSpeed_sq
declarations.statement:
lemma circularSpeed_sq {mu R : ℝ} (hm : 0 < mu) (hR : 0 < R) :
    circularSpeed mu R ^ 2 = mu/R

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.circularSpeed_eq_rate
declarations.statement:
lemma circularSpeed_eq_rate {mu R : ℝ} (hm : 0 < mu) (hR : 0 < R) :
    R*circularRate mu R = circularSpeed mu R

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.norm_circularPosition
declarations.statement:
lemma norm_circularPosition {mu R : ℝ} (hR : 0 < R) (phase t : ℝ) :
    ‖circularPosition mu R phase t‖ = R

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.hasDerivAt_circularPosition
declarations.statement:
lemma hasDerivAt_circularPosition (mu R phase t : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (circularPosition mu R phase) (circularVelocity mu R phase t) t

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.hasDerivAt_circularVelocity
declarations.statement:
lemma hasDerivAt_circularVelocity (mu R phase t : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (circularVelocity mu R phase)
      (-(circularRate mu R)^2 • circularPosition mu R phase t) t

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.circular_newton
declarations.statement:
lemma circular_newton {mu R : ℝ} (hm : 0 < mu) (hR : 0 < R)
    (phase t : ℝ) :
    deriv (deriv (circularPosition mu R phase)) t =
      -(mu/‖circularPosition mu R phase t‖^3) • circularPosition mu R phase t

modules.title: Time derivatives of the Hohmann ellipse
modules.doc:
Kepler time determines the velocity and acceleration.

## i. Overview

The inverse Kepler clock supplies the anomaly rate. Differentiating the Cartesian coordinates
yields the velocity and then an acceleration parallel to the displacement.

## ii. Key results

- `hasDerivAt_velocity` gives the main result of this module.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Differentiation along the ellipse

## iv. References

- [ref: hohmann_jpl_orbital_mechanics] describes the Hohmann ellipse and its apses.

declarations.doc: The position on the transfer ellipse at the given physical time.
declarations.statement: def position (p : Parameters) (t : ℝ) : ℂ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.velocity
declarations.doc: The velocity on the transfer ellipse at a given physical time.
declarations.statement: def velocity (p : Parameters) (t : ℝ) : ℂ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.hasDerivAt_D
declarations.statement:
lemma hasDerivAt_D (p : Parameters) (u : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (D p) (p.e*Real.sin u) u

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.hasDerivAt_position
declarations.statement:
lemma hasDerivAt_position (p : Parameters) (t : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (position p) (velocity p t) t

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.hasDerivAt_velocityAtAnomaly_x
declarations.statement:
lemma hasDerivAt_velocityAtAnomaly_x (p : Parameters) (u : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (fun s => (velocityAtAnomaly p s).re)
      (-p.a*p.n*(Real.cos u-p.e)/(D p u)^2) u

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.hasDerivAt_velocityAtAnomaly_y
declarations.statement:
lemma hasDerivAt_velocityAtAnomaly_y (p : Parameters) (u : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (fun s => (velocityAtAnomaly p s).im)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.hasDerivAt_velocity
declarations.statement:
lemma hasDerivAt_velocity (p : Parameters) (t : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (velocity p)

modules.title: Newtonian dynamics of the Hohmann ellipse
modules.doc:
The transfer coast solves the inverse-square equation.

## i. Overview

The norm of the position stays positive. Rewriting the radial acceleration with the mean motion
law gives the Newtonian acceleration at every real time.

## ii. Key results

- `second_deriv_position` gives the main result of this module.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The Newtonian equation and periodicity

## iv. References

- [ref: hohmann_jpl_orbital_mechanics] describes the Hohmann ellipse and its apses.

sections.text: ## A. The Newtonian equation and periodicity

declarations.statement:
lemma norm_position (p : Parameters) (t : ℝ) :
    ‖position p t‖ = radial p (anomaly p t)

declarations.statement:
lemma position_bounds (p : Parameters) (t : ℝ) :
    p.r₁ ≤ ‖position p t‖ ∧ ‖position p t‖ ≤ p.r₂

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.norm_position_pos
declarations.statement: lemma norm_position_pos (p : Parameters) (t : ℝ) : 0 < ‖position p t‖

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.position_ne_zero
declarations.statement: lemma position_ne_zero (p : Parameters) (t : ℝ) : position p t ≠ 0

declarations.statement:
lemma acceleration_coefficient (p : Parameters) (u : ℝ) :
    p.n^2/(D p u)^3 = p.mu/(radial p u)^3

lemma hasDerivAt_velocity_newton (p : Parameters) (t : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (velocity p) (gravity p.mu (position p t)) t

declarations.statement:
lemma second_deriv_position (p : Parameters) (t : ℝ) :
    deriv (deriv (position p)) t = -(p.mu/‖position p t‖^3) • position p t

modules.title: Apsidal speeds on the Hohmann ellipse
modules.doc:
The transfer velocity is tangential at both apses.

## i. Overview

Evaluating the actual time derivative at departure and arrival gives the periapsis and apoapsis
speeds. These speeds admit closed forms in the two orbital radii.

## ii. Key results

- `periSpeed_formula` gives the main result of this module.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Positions and velocities at the apses

## iv. References

- [ref: hohmann_jpl_orbital_mechanics] describes the Hohmann ellipse and its apses.

sections.text: ## A. Positions and velocities at the apses

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.periSpeed
declarations.doc: The transfer speed at periapsis.
declarations.statement: def periSpeed (p : Parameters) : ℝ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.apoSpeed
declarations.doc: The transfer speed at apoapsis.
declarations.statement: def apoSpeed (p : Parameters) : ℝ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.periSpeed_pos
declarations.statement: lemma periSpeed_pos (p : Parameters) : 0 < periSpeed p

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.apoSpeed_pos
declarations.statement: lemma apoSpeed_pos (p : Parameters) : 0 < apoSpeed p

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.position_departure
declarations.statement: lemma position_departure (p : Parameters) : position p 0 = pack p.r₁ 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.position_arrival
declarations.statement:
lemma position_arrival (p : Parameters) :
    position p p.transferTime = pack (-p.r₂) 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.velocity_departure
declarations.statement: lemma velocity_departure (p : Parameters) : velocity p 0 = pack 0 (periSpeed p)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.velocity_arrival
declarations.statement:
lemma velocity_arrival (p : Parameters) :
    velocity p p.transferTime = pack 0 (-apoSpeed p)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.periSpeed_sq
declarations.statement:
lemma periSpeed_sq (p : Parameters) :
    periSpeed p ^ 2 = 2*p.mu*p.r₂/(p.r₁*(p.r₁+p.r₂))

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.apoSpeed_sq
declarations.statement:
lemma apoSpeed_sq (p : Parameters) :
    apoSpeed p ^ 2 = 2*p.mu*p.r₁/(p.r₂*(p.r₁+p.r₂))

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.periSpeed_formula
declarations.statement:
lemma periSpeed_formula (p : Parameters) :
    periSpeed p = Real.sqrt (2*p.mu*p.r₂/(p.r₁*(p.r₁+p.r₂)))

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.apoSpeed_formula
declarations.statement:
lemma apoSpeed_formula (p : Parameters) :
    apoSpeed p = Real.sqrt (2*p.mu*p.r₁/(p.r₂*(p.r₁+p.r₂)))

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.norm_velocity_departure
declarations.statement: lemma norm_velocity_departure (p : Parameters) : ‖velocity p 0‖ = periSpeed p

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.norm_velocity_arrival
declarations.statement:
lemma norm_velocity_arrival (p : Parameters) :
    ‖velocity p p.transferTime‖ = apoSpeed p

modules.title: Geometry of the Hohmann ellipse
modules.doc:
The eccentric anomaly parameterizes the transfer ellipse.

## i. Overview

The attracting centre is at the origin. The distance from the focus lies between the two circular
radii, with equality at the two apses.

## ii. Key results

- `norm_ellipse` gives the main result of this module.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The ellipse and its apses

## iv. References

- [ref: hohmann_jpl_orbital_mechanics] describes the Hohmann ellipse and its apses.

modules.title: The two Hohmann velocity impulses
modules.doc:
The velocity jumps match the transfer ellipse to the circles.

## i. Overview

The two velocity jumps are tangential. Their magnitudes are the speed excess at departure and the
speed deficit at arrival. At the opposite apsis the prograde direction is the negative imaginary
axis.

## ii. Key results

- `totalDeltaV_eq_sum_norms` gives the main result of this module.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Vector jumps and their magnitudes

## iv. References

- [ref: hohmann_jpl_orbital_mechanics] describes the Hohmann ellipse and its apses.

sections.text: ## A. Vector jumps and their magnitudes

declarations.statement: def deltaV₁ (p : Parameters) : ℝ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.peri_excess_sq
declarations.statement:
lemma peri_excess_sq (p : Parameters) :
    periSpeed p ^ 2 - circularSpeed p.mu p.r₁ ^ 2 =
      p.mu*(p.r₂-p.r₁)/(p.r₁*(p.r₁+p.r₂))

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.apo_deficit_sq
declarations.statement:
lemma apo_deficit_sq (p : Parameters) :
    circularSpeed p.mu p.r₂ ^ 2 - apoSpeed p ^ 2 =
      p.mu*(p.r₂-p.r₁)/(p.r₂*(p.r₁+p.r₂))

declarations.statement: lemma deltaV₁_pos (p : Parameters) : 0 < deltaV₁ p

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.deltaV₂_pos
declarations.statement: lemma deltaV₂_pos (p : Parameters) : 0 < deltaV₂ p

declarations.statement: lemma totalDeltaV_pos (p : Parameters) : 0 < totalDeltaV p

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.periSpeed_factorized
declarations.statement:
lemma periSpeed_factorized (p : Parameters) :
    periSpeed p = circularSpeed p.mu p.r₁ * Real.sqrt (2*p.r₂/(p.r₁+p.r₂))

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.apoSpeed_factorized
declarations.statement:
lemma apoSpeed_factorized (p : Parameters) :
    apoSpeed p = circularSpeed p.mu p.r₂ * Real.sqrt (2*p.r₁/(p.r₁+p.r₂))

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.deltaV₁_formula
declarations.statement:
lemma deltaV₁_formula (p : Parameters) :
    deltaV₁ p = Real.sqrt (p.mu/p.r₁) *
      (Real.sqrt (2*p.r₂/(p.r₁+p.r₂))-1)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.deltaV₂_formula
declarations.statement:
lemma deltaV₂_formula (p : Parameters) :
    deltaV₂ p = Real.sqrt (p.mu/p.r₂) *
      (1-Real.sqrt (2*p.r₁/(p.r₁+p.r₂)))

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.entryImpulse_eq
declarations.statement: lemma entryImpulse_eq (p : Parameters) : entryImpulse p = pack 0 (deltaV₁ p)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.exitImpulse_eq
declarations.statement: lemma exitImpulse_eq (p : Parameters) : exitImpulse p = pack 0 (-deltaV₂ p)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.entryImpulse_norm
declarations.statement: lemma entryImpulse_norm (p : Parameters) : ‖entryImpulse p‖ = deltaV₁ p

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.exitImpulse_norm
declarations.statement: lemma exitImpulse_norm (p : Parameters) : ‖exitImpulse p‖ = deltaV₂ p

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.totalDeltaV_eq_sum_norms
declarations.statement:
lemma totalDeltaV_eq_sum_norms (p : Parameters) :
    totalDeltaV p = ‖entryImpulse p‖ + ‖exitImpulse p‖

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.impulses_tangential
declarations.statement:
lemma impulses_tangential (p : Parameters) :
    (position p 0).re * (entryImpulse p).re +
      (position p 0).im * (entryImpulse p).im = 0 ∧
    (position p p.transferTime).re * (exitImpulse p).re +
      (position p p.transferTime).im * (exitImpulse p).im = 0

modules.title: Mechanical invariants of the Hohmann ellipse
modules.doc:
The elliptical coast has constant specific energy and angular momentum.

## i. Overview

The squared speed follows the vis-viva identity. Together with the focus distance and the planar
cross product this gives the conserved specific energy and signed angular momentum.

## ii. Key results

- `coast_energy` gives the main result of this module.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Vis-viva and the two invariants

## iv. References

- [ref: hohmann_jpl_orbital_mechanics] describes the Hohmann ellipse and its apses.

sections.text: ## A. Vis-viva and the two invariants

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.specificEnergy
declarations.doc: The sum of kinetic and gravitational potential energy per unit mass.
declarations.statement: def specificEnergy (mu : ℝ) (q v : ℂ) : ℝ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.velocity_numerator
declarations.statement:
lemma velocity_numerator (p : Parameters) (u : ℝ) :
    p.a^2*Real.sin u^2 + p.b^2*Real.cos u^2 =
      p.a^2 * D p u * (1+p.e*Real.cos u)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.velocityAtAnomaly_norm_sq
declarations.statement:
lemma velocityAtAnomaly_norm_sq (p : Parameters) (u : ℝ) :
    ‖velocityAtAnomaly p u‖^2 =
      p.n^2*p.a^2*(1+p.e*Real.cos u)/D p u

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.vis_viva_at_anomaly
declarations.statement:
lemma vis_viva_at_anomaly (p : Parameters) (u : ℝ) :
    ‖velocityAtAnomaly p u‖^2 = p.mu*(2/‖ellipse p u‖-1/p.a)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.vis_viva
declarations.statement:
lemma vis_viva (p : Parameters) (t : ℝ) :
    ‖deriv (position p) t‖^2 = p.mu*(2/‖position p t‖-1/p.a)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.coast_energy
declarations.statement:
lemma coast_energy (p : Parameters) (t : ℝ) :
    specificEnergy p.mu (position p t) (deriv (position p) t) = -p.mu/(2*p.a)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.coast_energy_negative
declarations.statement:
lemma coast_energy_negative (p : Parameters) (t : ℝ) :
    specificEnergy p.mu (position p t) (deriv (position p) t) < 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.angular_momentum_at_anomaly
declarations.statement:
lemma angular_momentum_at_anomaly (p : Parameters) (u : ℝ) :
    cross (ellipse p u) (velocityAtAnomaly p u) = p.a*p.b*p.n

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.coast_angular_momentum
declarations.statement:
lemma coast_angular_momentum (p : Parameters) (t : ℝ) :
    cross (position p t) (deriv (position p) t) = p.a*p.b*p.n

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.coast_angular_momentum_pos
declarations.statement:
lemma coast_angular_momentum_pos (p : Parameters) (t : ℝ) :
    0 < cross (position p t) (deriv (position p) t)

modules.title: Kepler time for the Hohmann ellipse
modules.doc:
The eccentric anomaly is obtained by inverting Kepler time.

## i. Overview

The derivative of the clock is strictly positive for eccentricity below one. Monotonicity and
surjectivity give an inverse on all real times, whose derivative follows from the inverse rule.

## ii. Key results

- `hasDerivAt_anomaly` gives the main result of this module.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The clock and its inverse

## iv. References

- [ref: hohmann_jpl_orbital_mechanics] describes the Hohmann ellipse and its apses.

modules.title: Lagrangian dynamics of the Hohmann transfer coast
modules.doc:
The smooth coast satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation for a Kepler Lagrangian on its radial range.

## i. Overview

The inverse-radius term is singular at the centre. The normed-space constructor for
`LagrangianSystem` requires a globally smooth Lagrangian. We smooth the inverse-radius term inside
half the inner orbital radius. The entire transfer ellipse stays outside this region, where the
Lagrangian is the usual kinetic term plus the gravitational parameter divided by the radius.

## ii. Key results

- `lagrangianSystem` packages the smooth extension on the planar configuration space.
- `lagrangianSystem_coord_eq` recovers the Kepler Lagrangian outside the modified region.
- `eulerLagrange_position` proves that the Euler–Lagrange covector vanishes on the smooth coast.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The Lagrangian on the plane
- B. The Euler–Lagrange equation along the coast

## iv. References

- [ref: hohmann_jpl_orbital_mechanics] describes the Hohmann transfer coast.

sections.text: ## A. The Lagrangian on the plane
## B. The Euler–Lagrange equation along the coast

declarations.statement:

    eulerLagrange (lagrangianSystem p) t₀ (position p) t = 0

The two circular radii determine the transfer ellipse.

The central gravitational parameter and the two radii determine the semiaxes, eccentricity, mean

## ii. Key results

## iii. Table of contents

modules.title: Planar coordinates for the Hohmann transfer
modules.doc:
Complex coordinates carry the Euclidean norm.

## i. Overview

The real and imaginary parts represent Cartesian coordinates. The norm and derivative identities
let later modules work with both components while retaining the Euclidean norm.

## ii. Key results

- `pack_deriv` gives the main result of this module.

## iii. Table of contents

## iv. References

modules.title: Existence of an outward Hohmann transfer
modules.doc:
Two positive ordered radii admit a tangential two-impulse transfer.

## i. Overview

The explicit ellipse joins two prograde circles at its apses. The statement exposes the time
derivatives, Newtonian equations, velocity jump norms, and transfer time in terms of the input
data.

## ii. Key results

- `exists_hohmann_transfer` gives the main result of this module.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Existence and physical transfer identities

## iv. References

- [ref: hohmann_jpl_orbital_mechanics] describes the Hohmann ellipse and its apses.

sections.text: ## A. Existence and physical transfer identities

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.hohmann_transfer
declarations.doc: The explicit outward transfer satisfies the Newtonian equations and burn identities.
declarations.statement:
lemma hohmann_transfer (p : Parameters) :
    0 < p.transferTime ∧
    (∀ t, deriv (deriv (position p)) t =
      -(p.mu/‖position p t‖^3) • position p t) ∧
    (∀ t, p.r₁ ≤ ‖position p t‖ ∧ ‖position p t‖ ≤ p.r₂) ∧
    position p 0 = pack p.r₁ 0 ∧
    position p p.transferTime = pack (-p.r₂) 0 ∧
    deriv (position p) 0 = pack 0 (periSpeed p) ∧
    deriv (position p) p.transferTime = pack 0 (-apoSpeed p) ∧
    incoming p 0 = position p 0 ∧
    position p p.transferTime = outgoing p p.transferTime ∧
    (∀ t, deriv (deriv (incoming p)) t =
      -(p.mu/‖incoming p t‖^3) • incoming p t) ∧
    (∀ t, deriv (deriv (outgoing p)) t =
      -(p.mu/‖outgoing p t‖^3) • outgoing p t) ∧
    ‖deriv (position p) 0-deriv (incoming p) 0‖ = deltaV₁ p ∧
    ‖deriv (outgoing p) p.transferTime-deriv (position p) p.transferTime‖ = deltaV₂ p ∧
    0 < deltaV₁ p ∧ 0 < deltaV₂ p ∧
    deltaV₁ p = Real.sqrt (p.mu/p.r₁)*(Real.sqrt (2*p.r₂/(p.r₁+p.r₂))-1) ∧
    deltaV₂ p = Real.sqrt (p.mu/p.r₂)*(1-Real.sqrt (2*p.r₁/(p.r₁+p.r₂))) ∧
    p.transferTime = Real.pi*Real.sqrt (p.a^3/p.mu) ∧
    (∀ t, specificEnergy p.mu (position p t) (deriv (position p) t) = -p.mu/(2*p.a)) ∧
    (∀ t, cross (position p t) (deriv (position p) t) = p.a*p.b*p.n)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.HohmannTransfer.exists_hohmann_transfer
declarations.doc:
Existence without asking the reader to trust a project-defined orbit predicate.
All geometric and motion hypotheses are consequences, not input fields.
declarations.statement:
lemma exists_hohmann_transfer (mu r₁ r₂ : ℝ)
    (hmu : 0 < mu) (hr₁ : 0 < r₁) (horder : r₁ < r₂) :
    ∃ (q v c₁ c₂ : ℝ → ℂ) (τ d₁ d₂ : ℝ),
      0 < τ ∧ 0 < d₁ ∧ 0 < d₂ ∧
      (∀ t, HasDerivAt q (v t) t) ∧
      (∀ t, HasDerivAt v (-(mu/‖q t‖^3) • q t) t) ∧
      (∀ t, deriv (deriv q) t = -(mu/‖q t‖^3) • q t) ∧
      (∀ t, r₁ ≤ ‖q t‖ ∧ ‖q t‖ ≤ r₂) ∧
      q 0 = pack r₁ 0 ∧ q τ = pack (-r₂) 0 ∧
      (∀ t, ‖c₁ t‖ = r₁) ∧ (∀ t, ‖c₂ t‖ = r₂) ∧
      (∀ t, deriv (deriv c₁) t = -(mu/‖c₁ t‖^3) • c₁ t) ∧
      (∀ t, deriv (deriv c₂) t = -(mu/‖c₂ t‖^3) • c₂ t) ∧
      c₁ 0 = q 0 ∧ q τ = c₂ τ ∧
      v 0-deriv c₁ 0 = pack 0 d₁ ∧
      deriv c₂ τ-v τ = pack 0 (-d₂) ∧
      ‖v 0-deriv c₁ 0‖ = d₁ ∧ ‖deriv c₂ τ-v τ‖ = d₂ ∧
      d₁ = Real.sqrt (mu/r₁)*(Real.sqrt (2*r₂/(r₁+r₂))-1) ∧
      d₂ = Real.sqrt (mu/r₂)*(1-Real.sqrt (2*r₁/(r₁+r₂))) ∧
      τ = Real.pi*Real.sqrt (((r₁+r₂)/2)^3/mu)

modules.title: Joining the Hohmann coast to circular orbits
modules.doc:
The incoming circle, transfer ellipse and outgoing circle share the burn positions.

## i. Overview

Each coast is defined on all real times. The flight uses them on successive intervals, with the
positions matched at the two impulses and velocities allowed to jump.

## ii. Key results

- `junction_velocity_jumps` gives the main result of this module.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Coast arcs and their junctions

## iv. References

- [ref: hohmann_jpl_orbital_mechanics] describes the Hohmann ellipse and its apses.

modules.title: The cost of a finite bielliptic transfer
modules.doc:
A third burn can reduce total impulse for a finite radius ratio.

## i. Overview

In normalized units the radii are 1, 64 and 16. Rational bounds on three square roots certify a
strict margin greater than 9/1000 in the summed speed changes.

## ii. Key results

- `Bielliptic.finite_bielliptic_saves_deltaV` gives the main result of this module.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The three-burn cost and its strict margin

## iv. References

- [ref: hohmann_weber_bielliptic]. Weber describes the three-burn bielliptic transfer geometry.

sections.text: ## A. The three-burn cost and its strict margin
